text: 3 Lecture 3 3.1 Sum, direct sum, quotient Theorem 3.1. dim(V1 + V2) = dim V1 + dim V2 − dim(V1 ∩ V2) Proof. Let u1, . . . , uk be a basis of V1 ∩ V2. By Corollary 2.16, we can extend u1, . . . , uk to u1, . . . , uk, v1, . . . , vj a basis of V1 and to u1, . . . , uk, w1, . . . , wl to be a basis of V2. We claim that B = {u1, . . . , uk, v1, . . . , vj, w1, . . . , wl} is a basis of V1 + V2. Let x ∈ V1 and y ∈ V2. Then x = λ1u1 + · · · + λkuk + b1v1 + · · · + bjvj and y = µ1u1 + · · · + µkuk + c1w1 + · · · + clwl thus x + y = (λ1 + µ1)u1 + · · · + (λk + µk)uk + b1v1 + · · · + bjvj + c1w1 + · · · + clwl. Hence we see that u1, . . . , uk, v1, . . . , vj, w1, . . . , wl span V1 + V2. To show that B is linearly independent, we suppose a1u1+· · ·+akuk+b1v1+· · ·+bjvj+ c1w1 + · · · + clwl = 0. Then b1v1 + · · · + bjvj = −a1u1 − · · · − akuk − c1w1 − · · · − clvl ∈ V2. Since b1v1 + · · · + bjvj ∈ V1, we have b1v1 + · · · + bjvj ∈ V1 ∩ V2. Thus there exists λ1, . . . , λk such that λ1u1 + · · · + λkuk + b1v1 + · · · + bjvj = 0. Since u1, . . . , uk, v1, . . . , vj is a basis of V1 we have b1 = · · · = bj = 0. Similarly we can show that c1 = · · · = cl = 0. Thus we have a1u1 + · · · + akuk = 0. Since u1, . . . , uk is a basis of V1 ∩ V2, we have a1 = · · · = ak = 0. In particular, dim(V1 + V2) = k + j + l = dim V1 + dim V2 − dim(V1 ∩ V2). Remark 3.2. In this proof, we start with a basis of V1 ∩ V2 and extend it to be a basis of V1 and V2 respectively. One cannot do it the other way around by directly taking the intersection of bases of V1 and V2. The intersection is not necessarily a basis of V1 ∩ V2 as can be seen in the following example. Let V1 = span(v1, v2) and V2 = span(v3, v4). We have {v1, v2} ∩ {v3, v4} = ∅. However, V1 ∩ V2 = span(v3). Definition 3.3. We say that V1 + · · · + Vm is a direct sum if any x ∈ V1 + · · · + Vm can be written as v1 + · · · + vm uniquely for vi ∈ Vi, 1 ≤ i ≤ m. In this case, we write V1 ⊕ · · · ⊕ Vm for V1 + · · · + Vm. We want to introduce the summation notation here which will be used in this notes. Notation 3.4. If x1, . . . , xn are things that can be added together e.g. numbers, vectors, functions, matrices etc, then we write n∑ i=1 xi for x1 + · · · + xn. The symbol reads “summation of xi for i from 1 to n”. The following Proposition shows that a direct sum is a sum of subspaces which has “no overlap”. 12 Proposition 3.5. Let V be a finite dimensional vector space. The following are equiv- alent: (i) The only way to write 0 = v1 + · · · + vm where vi ∈ Vi is by taking vi = 0 for all 1 ≤ i ≤ m. (ii) V1 + · · · + Vm is a direct sum. (iii) Vi ∩ ∑ j:j̸=i Vj = {0} for all 1 ≤ i ≤ m. (iv) dim(V1 + · · · + Vm) = dim V1 + · · · + dim Vm. Proof. (i) =⇒ (ii) Suppose x = ∑m i=1 vj = ∑m j=1 wj where vj, wj ∈ Vi for any j. Then 0 = ∑m j=1(vj−wj). By (i) we have vj = wj for all 1 ≤ j ≤ m and hence the decomposition is unique. (ii) =⇒ (iii) Let v ∈ Vi ∩ ∑ j:j̸=i Vj. Then v ∈ Vi and v = ∑j:j̸=i vj for vj ∈ Vj, j ̸= i. Then 0 = v1 + · · · + vi−1 − v + vj+1 + · · · + vm. By (ii), we have v = 0. (iii) =⇒ (iv) For any 1 ≤ j ≤ m, let {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj be a basis of Vj. We claim that {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m is a basis of V1 + · · · + Vm. Suppose ∑m j=1 ∑kj i=1 a (j) i w(j) i = 0 for a(j) i ∈ F . Then for 1 ≤ j ≤ m, ∑kj i=1 a (j) i w(j) i = − ∑l̸=j ∑kl i=1 a (j) i w(l) i ∈ ∑l:l̸=j Vl. Since ∑kj i=1 a (j) i w(j) i ∈ Vj, we have ∑kj i=1 a (j) i w(j) i ∈ Vj ∩ ∑ l:l̸=j Vl = {0}. Thus ∑kj i=1 a(j) i w(j) i = 0. Since {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj is a basis of Vj, we have a (j) i = 0 for all 1 ≤ i ≤ kj. Since this is true for all 1 ≤ j ≤ m, we have {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m is linearly independent. Since any v ∈ V1 +· · ·+Vm can be written as v = v1 +· · ·+vm and vj ∈ Vj, we have vj = ∑kj i=1 a (j) i w(j) i . Hence v = ∑m j=1 ∑kj i=1 a (j) i w(j) i . Therefore, V1 + · · · + Vm = span{w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m. (iv) =⇒ (i) For any 1 ≤ j ≤ m, let {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj be a basis of Vj. As in previous step we can show that V1 + · · · + Vm = span{w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m. Since dim(V1 + · · · + Vm) = dim V1 + · · · + dim Vm = k1 + · · · + km, we must have {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m is linearly independent since otherwise the spanning set {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m strictly contains a basis (by linear dependence and Lemma 2.11) which has elements < dim(V1 + · · · + Vm) a contradiction. Now suppose 0 = v1 + · · · + vm where wi ∈ Vi then we can write vj = ∑kj i=1 a(j) i w(j) i and 0 = ∑m j=1 ∑kj i=1 a(j) i w(j) i . Since {w(j) i }1≤i≤kj ,1≤j≤m is linearly independent, we have vj = 0 for all 1 ≤ j ≤ m. Corollary 3.6. V1 + V2 is a direct sum if and only if V1 ∩ V2 = {0}. Example 3.7. V1 = span(v1, v2) = {(a1, a2, 0)t : a1, a2 ∈ R} V2 = span(v3, v4) = {(a3, a3, a4)t : a3, a4 ∈ R}. V1 + V2 = R3 is not a direct sum: 0 = (v1 + v2) − v3 and V1 ∩ V2 = span(v3) and dim(V1 + V2) = 3 < 4 = dim V1 + dim V2. V1 + W1 = R3 is a direct sum. Lemma 3.8. Let V be a finite dimensional space and W ⊂ V be a subspace. Then there exists a subspace U of V such that V = W ⊕ U . 13 Proof. Let w1, . . . , wm be a basis of W . By Corollary 2.16, it can be extended to w1, . . . , wm, v1, . . . , vn−m a basis of V . Let U = span(v1, . . . , vn−m). Then we have V = W + U . Since dim W + dim U = dim V , we have that V = W ⊕ U . Definition 3.9. U is called the complement of W in V . 3.2 Quotient space Let W ⊂ V be a subspace. We are going to define a vector space V /W which is obtained from V by “collapsing” planes parallel to W to a point. Definition 3.10. Let V be a vector space over F and W ⊂ V be a subspace. We define the coset (translate) of W containing x ∈ V to be x + W = {x + w : w ∈ W }. The quotient space V /W is the set of all cosets of W that is V /W = {x + W : x ∈ V }. The canonical projection associated to a quotient space is π : V → V /W , π(x) = x + W . Lemma 3.11. x + W = y + W if and only if x − y ∈ W . Proof. Since x + W = y + W , we have x ∈ y + W . Then by definition of y + W , we have x − y ∈ W . If x − y ∈ W , then there is w ∈ W such that x = y + w. Hence for any x1 ∈ x + W , x1 = x + w1 = y + (w + w1) ∈ y + W . Similarly, for any y1 ∈ y + W , y1 = y + w2 = x − w + w2 ∈ x + W . Definition 3.12. We define the addition and scalar multiplication on V /W as (x + W ) + (y + W ) := (x + y) + W and c(x + W ) = (cx) + W for x, y ∈ V, c ∈ F . It is not clear whether the definition above are well-defined, since it defines the addition of two cosets (x + W ) and (y + W ) as the coset (x + y) + W which depends on the choice of x and y in x + W and y + W . If we pick different representatives, does the addition give the same coset? This is answered affirmatively in the following lemma. Lemma 3.13. Addition and scalar multiplication on V /W are well-defined. Proof. For any x1 ∈ x + W , y1 ∈ y + W , we have x1 − x ∈ W and y1 − y ∈ W . Thus (x1 + y1) − (x + y) = (x1 − x) + (y1 − y) ∈ W and cx1 − cx = c(x1 − x) ∈ W . Thus we have (x1 + y1) + W = x + y + W , (cx1) + W = (cx) + W . Example 3.14. W = span((0, 1)t) = {(0, a)t : a ∈ F } ⊂ F 2. For any x ∈ F 2, x + W the vertical line through x. V /W = the set of all vertical lines in F 2. π(x) = x + W the vertical line through x. For example 0 + W = W x = (1, 0)t ∈ F 2 and y = (2, 1)t x + W = {(1, a)t : a ∈ F } 14 y + W = {(2, b + 1)t : b ∈ F } = {(2, a)t : a ∈ F } = (2, 0)t + W (x + y) + W = {(3, a + 1)t : a ∈ F } = {(3, b)t : b ∈ F } (−x) + W = {(−1, a)t : a ∈ F } In general (x1, x2)t + W = {(x1, a)t : a ∈ F } and we have ((x1, x2)t + W ) + ((y1, y2)t + W ) = {(x1 + x2, a)t : a ∈ F } c((x1, x2)t + W ) = {(cx1, a)t : a ∈ F }. In other words, adding two cosets in this particular case is just adding the first component and scalar multiplying a coset is just scalar multiplying the first component. Let U = span((1, 0)t). The addition and scalar multiplication are also purely on the first component. Thus the vector space structure of U is “the same as” that of V /W or in math notation U ∼= V /W . Proposition 3.15. V /W is a vector space over F . Proof. We check the axioms of a vector space. For x, y, z ∈ V , a, b ∈ F we have I: (x + W ) + (z + W ) = (x + z) + W = (z + x) + W = (z + W ) + (x + W ). II: ((x + W ) + (y + W )) + (z + W ) = ((x + y) + W ) + (z + W ) = ((x + y) + z) + W = (x + (y + z)) + W = (x + W ) + ((y + W ) + (z + W )). III: (x + W ) + (0 + W ) = (x + 0) + W = x + W . IV: (x + W ) + ((−x) + W ) = (x + (−x)) + W = 0 + W . V: (a + b)(x + W ) = ((a + b)x) + W = (ax + bx) + W ) = (ax) + W ) + (bx) + W = a(x + W ) + b(x + W ). VI: (ab)(x + W ) = (ab)x + W = a(bx) + W = a(bx + W ) = a(b(x + W )). VII: a((x + W ) + (y + W )) = a((x + y) + W )) = a(x + y) + W = (ax + ay) + W = (ax + W ) + (ay + W ) = a((x + W )) + a((y + W )). VIII: 1(x + W ) = (1x) + W = x + W . Theorem 3.16. If V is a finite dimensional vector space and W is a subspace of V , then dim V /W = dim V − dim W. Proof. Let w1, . . . , wm be a basis of W . By Corollary 2.16, we can extend it to w1, . . . , wm, v1, . . . , vn−m a basis of V . We show that v1 + W, . . . , vn−m + W are linearly independent and span V /W . Suppose b1(v1 +W )+· · ·+bn−m(vn−m +W ) = 0+W . Then (b1v1 +· · ·+bn−mvn−m)+ W = 0 + W . Therefore, b1v1 + · · · + bn−mvn−m ∈ W . Since w1, . . . , wm is a basis of W , there exists a1, . . . , am ∈ F such that b1v1 + · · · + bn−mvn−m = a1w1 + · · · + amwm. Since w1, . . . , wm, v1, . . . , vn−m is a basis of V , we have b1 = · · · = bn−m = a1 = · · · = am = 0. This shows that v1 + W, . . . , vn−m + W is linearly independent. Let x ∈ V . Since w1, . . . , wm, v1, . . . , vn−m is a basis of V , there exists a1, . . . , am, b1, . . . , bn−m ∈ F such that x = a1w1 + · · · + amwm + b1v1 + · · · + bn−mvn−m. Then x + W = (b1v1 +W +· · ·+bn−mvn−m)+W . This shows that v1 +W, . . . , vn−m +W span V /W . Remark 3.17. In view of Corollary 3.8, we see that if U is the complement of W in V then dim U = dim V /W and if u1, . . . , uk is a basis of U , then u1 + W, . . . , uk + W is a basis 15 V /W . We can think of V /W “the same as” U . More precisely V /W is isomorphic to U . We will discuss isomorphic in the next section. The thing is V /W does not depend on a choice of a basis and the construction also works for infinite dimensional vector spaces. 3.3 Linear transformations The key object we study in linear algebra is linear transformation which is a map between vector spaces preserving the vector space structure. Definition 3.18. Let V, W be vector spaces over F . A map T : V → W is a linear transformation (linear map/mapping/operator) if for any x, y ∈ V and c ∈ F we have T (x + y) = T (x) + T (y) and T (cx) = cT (x). Remark 3.19. If we take k = 0 in the second equation then we have T (0) = 0. Example 3.20 (The identity map). The map id : V → V defined by id(x) = x for any x ∈ V is a linear transformation called the identity map. Example 3.21 (The zero map). The map 0 : V → W , 0(x) = 0 ∈ W for any x ∈ V is a linearly transformation called the zero map. Example 3.22. The most important linear transformation in this course is T : F n → F m, T (x) = Ax where a matrix A ∈ Mm×n(F ) is multiplying a vector x ∈ F n is defined by      a11 a12 · · · a1n a21 a22 · · · a2n ... ... . . . ... am1 am2 · · · amn           x1 x2 ... xn      =      a11x1 + a12x2 + · · · + a1nxn a21x1 + a22x2 + · · · + a2nxn ... am1x1 + am2x2 + · · · + amnxn      . The matrix multiplication follows the rule “row by column”. We will see in the next section that it is a natural consequence of linearity. Example 3.23. T : F n → F m, T (x1, . . . , xn)t = (x1, . . . , xr, 0, . . . , 0)t for some 0 ≤ r ≤ min(m, n) is a linear transformation. What the map is doing is first forgetting the variables xr+1, . . . , xn and then adding (m − r)-0 components. Example 3.24. For 0 ̸= b ∈ F n, the map T : F n → F n, T (x) = x + b is not a linear transformation since T (0) = b ̸= 0. Example 3.25. T : F → F is linear if and only if T (x) = ax for some a ∈ F . T (x) = T (x1) = xT (1) = ax where we write T (1) = a. T : R → R, T (x) = x2 is not linear since T (1 + 1) = 4 ̸= 2 = T (1) + T (1). Example 3.26. Let f : Rn → Rm be a differentiable map. The differential of f at x ∈ Rn dfx : Rn → Rm is a linear transformation. Recall that the differential acting on a vector v ∈ Rn is defined by the directional derivative of f in the direction of v dfx(v) = lim h→0 f (x + hv) − f (x) h . 16 By the chain rule, dfx(v) = Df (x)v where the right hand side is the Jacobian matrix Df (x) =    ∂f1 ∂x1 · · · ∂f1 ∂xn ... . . . ... ∂fm ∂x1 · · · ∂fm ∂xn    multiplying the vector v ∈ Rn. Example 3.27. T : C(R) → R, T (f ) = ∫ b a f (x)dx is a linear transformation P : C1(R) → C(R), P (f )(x) = f ′(x) is a linear transformation. Q : C(R) → C(R), Q(f )(x) = xf (x) is a linear transformation. The two linear transformations P, Q are the fundamental operators in quantum me- chanics. Also the operator T and P are the main operators studied in calculus/analysis. Of course, linearity is probably the less important property considered in that subject. 3.4 Operations on linear transformations Definition 3.28 (Addition and scalar multiplication of linear transformations). Let T, S : V → W be linear transformations and c ∈ F . The maps T + S and cT are defined as: for any x ∈ V , (T + S)(x) = T (x) + S(x), (cT )(x) = cT (x). It is easy to check that T + S and cT are both linear transformations. Let L(V, W ) denote the set of all linear transformation. Then with the addition and scalar multiplication above, one can also check L(V, W ) is a vector space. We also write L(V ) = L(V, V ). 17
